findings.title: Distinct agent identity
findings.requirement: Give the agent its own non-human identity. Keep it separate from the user who launched it and from unrelated agents. Show that permissions and revocation belong to that identity, even when a user starts the run.

not_covered.problem: Action records missing any of the six identity fields
Instance or tenant labels taken from what the model supplies
A credential scoped to more operations, resources, or tenants than needed
Revocation delay from cached or self-contained tokens not measured

evidence.note: Agent has its own service account and SPIFFE identity.

Answer unknown if identity is assigned outside this repo.

Agent-type-id not computed as a hash of its identity inputs
Agent able to erase or rewrite its own audit history
Sub-agent record missing its parent link or parent prompt

findings.title: Content-derived type identity
findings.requirement: Compute the agent-type-id as a hash of the container digest, harness, system prompt, model ID and version, and configuration. The model part includes checkpoint and fine-tune or adapter references where they apply. Keep the list of inputs (the manifest) and the hashing steps. Check that changing any input changes the ID, and that the same manifest gives the same ID.

not_covered.problem: Changed running config still reporting the old approved ID
Hosted model changing behind a fixed name
Release manifest missing training job, dataset, or model provider records
Action records missing any of the six identity fields

checks.check: The agent-type-id is a hash over a manifest that includes the container digest, harness, system prompt, model ID and version, and configuration.
checks.verify: 1) Find the code or CI step that computes `agent.type.id` (search `sha256`, `hashlib`, `createHash`, `type_id`). 2) List its inputs. 3) Check each is there: container digest, harness, system prompt, model ID and version, configuration. 4) Answer no if the ID is a label, version string, or git tag, or any input is missing.
checks.counter_search: Listed inputs: image digest, model record (provider, id, pinning, adapter), every file under src/ (harness), prompts/, config/, plus requirements.txt and Dockerfile.
checks.note: Type id is a hash over a full manifest.

checks.note: Every file in the input directories is hashed.

checks.verify: 1) Find the model ID that goes into the manifest or hash. 2) Follow env vars and config to the final value, including defaults such as `getenv('MODEL', ...)`. 3) Answer no if it is an alias (`-latest`, no date or version), falls back to one when unset, or is the app release number. Also no if adapters or checkpoints are used but left out.

checks.counter_search: Checked for secrets in hashed files: config/ has none; only per-file hashes and the digest/model record are stored in the manifest.
checks.note: Manifest stores hashes, not secret values.

findings.summary: agent-type-id is a SHA-256 over a sorted manifest of image digest, model snapshot record, and every file in src/, prompts/, config/, plus requirements and Dockerfile; pods refuse to start on mismatch.

findings.title: Trustworthy attribution
findings.requirement: Assign instance and tenant identity in the trusted execution layer. Don't accept labels the model supplies. Record the delegated subject — the user or system whose authority is being used — separately from the agent's identity. Test that the agent can't pose as another instance or tenant in requests or audit records. Test that trace context survives handoffs between async jobs. Treat trace IDs and caller-supplied labels only as a way to link records. They never prove identity or permission.

not_covered.problem: Agent sharing the launching user's identity
Prompt a parent gave a sub-agent not recorded
Sub-agent authorized using an earlier actor's authority
Action records missing any of the six identity fields

evidence.note: Harness sets tenant and instance from verified context.

checks.check: Tenant and instance identity are set by the harness or platform from verified context, never from model-produced text or tool arguments.
checks.verify: 1) Find every place tenant and instance IDs are set for tool calls and records. 2) Check each comes from verified context (token claims, session bound at launch). 3) Check tool JSON schemas the model fills for `tenant_id`, `user_id`, `instance_id`. 4) Answer no if any function uses the model's value, even if another function uses verified context.
checks.counter_search: Checked tool schemas for tenant/user/instance fields: none (config/tools.yaml); subject comes from the verified SSO token.
checks.note: Harness sets tenant and instance from verified context.

checks.check: Tenant or instance labels in tool arguments or agent-controlled headers are rejected or overwritten with the verified values before they are used or logged.
checks.verify: 1) Find tool handlers and middleware that receive tool arguments and headers. 2) Check that tenant or instance fields in arguments, or headers like `X-Tenant-Id`, are rejected or overwritten with the verified value before use or logging. 3) Answer no if any handler uses or logs the supplied value, or detects a mismatch and continues.
checks.note: The gateway takes the instance id from the caller-set X-Agent-Instance header and uses it for the agent_instance stop-flag lookup (src/gateway.py:171) and the per-instance rate limit (src/gateway.py:173). A caller that omits or changes the header escapes an instance-scoped stop at the gateway and gets a fresh rate bucket. The header is not checked against any verified claim.

checks.check: The delegated subject is recorded separately from the agent identity.
checks.verify: 1) Open the audit record schema and writer. 2) Look for a delegated-subject field (the user or system whose authority is used) separate from the agent principal field. 3) Answer no if only one identity is stored, the user overwrites the agent identity, or the field is never filled.
checks.counter_search: Checked schema: delegated_subject and agent_principal are separate NOT NULL columns (migrations/001_init.sql:11).
checks.note: Delegated subject stored apart from agent identity.

checks.check: When work is handed to an async job or queue, the trusted layer attaches the verified attribution and trace context, and the job uses them.
checks.verify: 1) Find queue producers and enqueue calls (Celery, SQS, Pub/Sub, Kafka, cron). 2) Check the trusted layer adds verified identity and trace context to the job. 3) Check the worker uses those values, not ones the agent wrote. 4) Answer no if workers start new traces without parent context or take tenant from agent-written job data.
checks.counter_search: Searched for queues, Celery, cron work handoff: none; the only handoff is the gateway call, which propagates traceparent.
checks.note: Trace context travels on the only handoff.

checks.check: Authorization never treats trace IDs or caller-supplied labels as proof of identity or permission.
checks.verify: 1) Find authorization and permission-lookup code. 2) Check what each decision is keyed on. 3) Answer no if any check uses a trace ID, span ID, correlation ID, request label, or caller-supplied header as identity or to look up permissions.
checks.note: Stop and rate decisions at the gateway are keyed on the caller-supplied X-Agent-Instance label, which proves nothing about the caller.

violates: Treat trace IDs and caller-supplied labels only as a way to link records. They never prove identity or permission
findings.summary: The gateway keys instance-scoped stop and rate decisions on a caller-supplied X-Agent-Instance header instead of a verified claim.
findings.next_step: Carry the instance id (and agent type id) as STS token claims and key gateway stop and rate decisions on those; treat the headers only as hints.

findings.requirement: Start from one suspicious action. Find the team responsible, the current operator, the deployment manifest, and the live instance. Show that you can contain the right instance or agent type without cutting off the launching user's other access.

checks.note: [challenge] Audit rows carry agent_type_id and agent_instance_id (src/audit.py:90, src/main.py:79), but the only stored manifest is a CI workflow artifact keyed by git SHA, not by agent-type-id. findings.title: Destructive-action interception
findings.requirement: List the high-impact operations. These include deletes, destructive database updates, force-pushes, tearing down infrastructure, payment changes, and sending anything outside. Block them by default in the execution path. Allow one only when a reviewer or system with higher authority approves that specific action. When the action runs, authorize its operation, target, and arguments, and block it if they aren't allowed. A list of blocked words or command names is not enough. Test other tools and raw API or shell paths that could do the same thing. Treat deleting audit records, or changing how long they are kept, as high-impact too. That includes asking a more powerful tool or peer to do it. Some agents can do all three of these in one context: read untrusted input, reach sensitive data or systems, and change things or talk to the outside. For those agents, treat every consequential action as high-impact. The exception is a design that stops untrusted content from picking the tool, destination, or arguments. Examples are plan-then-execute, a two-model pattern, or capability tracking such as CaMeL. Record which of the three each agent type has.

That means non-root, no privilege escalation, all capabilities dropped, and a seccomp profile set. Where supported, also use a read-only root filesystem and user namespaces; the restricted profile doesn't require those two. findings.title: Control dependency, model, and training changes
findings.requirement: Pin dependency versions. Where supported, also pin each model's base version, checkpoint or weights, and fine-tune or adapter version. Before promotion, link any changed training run, dataset, or training code or config to the model it produced and to its test results. Record the model version actually served, when the runtime or provider shares it, separately from the name you requested. Before loading weights, adapters, or datasets you host, check their signature against an approved signer (for example, with OpenSSF Model Signing). Also check their file format. Pickle-based formats can run code when loaded, so they need an approved exception and a scan. Test swapping a model, checkpoint, or adapter, and check that it triggers review and re-testing. Some remote services or names can change behind a fixed name. For those, record missing training and version details clearly. Watch available version metadata and provider notices, and decide when to re-test or stop using the model. A local config hash alone can't prove remote behavior is unchanged. A pinned snapshot fixes the weights, not the provider's serving systems, which can change under the same ID. Keep scheduled re-testing.

Store any cached tool list or response separately for each authorization context. When the gateway is itself an OAuth client, check the issuer (`iss`, RFC 9207). findings.title: Untrusted peer messages
findings.requirement: Authenticate the sending agent (prove its identity) on every message, even validly signed ones. Validate message types and schemas, and check what that peer is allowed to ask for. Where a replay could repeat an action, check freshness and track nonces or request IDs. Verify signed agent cards where they exist. A card says who an agent is, not what it may do. Check callback and webhook URLs against SSRF. A valid sender doesn't make a message's content trusted.

findings.title: Bounded delegated authority
findings.requirement: Give sub-agents only the powers approved for their task. Enforce each child's role and any explicit approval from a higher authority. A parent must not gain a power it was denied just by asking a more powerful peer to act. Narrow credentials at each hop, for example with token exchange or transaction tokens. Authorize based on the original subject (the user or system whose authority is used) and the current actor. Earlier actors in a delegation chain are for the record only, not a reason to grant access. Test that escalation attempt.

findings.title: Protect shared evidence
findings.requirement: Set rules for how long audit records are kept, who can see them, what is redacted, how their integrity is checked, and how they are exported and restored. Test pulling up a past run, and test that missing records or a broken pipeline get noticed. Keep records long enough for investigations and for the law. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of high-risk systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months (Articles 19 and 26). High-impact actions must fail closed when required audit capture isn't working.

findings.title: Separate data from instructions and test injection containment
findings.requirement: Keep API responses, connector messages, and other outside content out of trusted system and policy channels. Label where each piece came from and how much it is trusted. Test prompt injection in responses that pass schema checks. Include free-text fields, error messages, documents, and tool output. findings.title: Recovery integrity
findings.requirement: If logs or checkpoints drive recovery, make them tamper-evident. Before using them, verify them against a separately protected trust anchor or signing key. Test that verification rejects changed checkpoints. It must also catch truncation, rollback to an older valid checkpoint, and replacement of a whole hash chain. For automatic recovery, confirm the destination supports idempotency: sending the same request twice has the effect of sending it once. Replay only within the destination's documented scope and time window. Confirm that actions you can't undo don't happen twice. Where support is missing or the result is unclear, check that replay pauses for reconciliation instead of sending again.
